Proposes that referential grounding requires two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories: causal-informational relations to the world and a history of selection that endows internal states with the function of carrying this information.
Argues that post-training (e.g., preference tuning for factual accuracy) can establish selection processes that confer world-involving representational functions to LLM internal states.
Suggests that pre-training might, under specific conditions, also lead to world-involving representational functions through implicit extra-linguistic success conditions in the training data.
Contends that in-context learning could, in principle, allow LLMs to acquire world-involving representational functions during inference without parameter updates.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) produce seemingly meaningful outputs, yet they are trained on text alone without direct interaction with the world. This leads to a modern variant of the classical symbol grounding problem in AI: can LLMs' internal states and outputs be about extra-linguistic reality, independently of the meaning human interpreters project onto them? We argue that they can. We first distinguish referential grounding -- the connection between a representation and its worldly referent -- from other forms of grounding and argue it is the only kind essential to solving the problem. We contend that referential grounding is achieved when a system's internal states satisfy two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories of representation: (1) they stand in appropriate causal-informational relations to the world, and (2) they have a history of selection that has endowed them with the function of carrying this information. We argue that LLMs can meet both conditions, even without multimodality or embodiment.

papers.title: Benchmarking explanation methods for mental state decoding with deep learning models
papers.research_question: How can we unify existing methods for interpreting model predictions and provide a unique solution with desirable properties?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SHAP, a unified framework for interpreting model predictions, which unifies six existing methods and provides a unique solution with desirable properties, along with new estimation methods that improve computational performance and consistency with human intuition.
papers.conclusion: SHAP provides a unified framework for interpreting model predictions, connecting existing methods and providing a unique solution with desirable properties, with promising future directions for faster estimation and integration of interaction effects.
papers.key_findings:
SHAP unifies six existing feature attribution methods (LIME, DeepLIFT, Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation, Shapley regression values, Shapley sampling values, Quantitative Input Influence) under a single class of additive feature attribution methods.
There is a unique solution in this class that satisfies three desirable properties: local accuracy, missingness, and consistency.
The SHAP values are the only feature attribution method that satisfies these properties.
Kernel SHAP provides more efficient estimation of SHAP values than previous sampling-based methods.
Deep SHAP, a compositional approximation for deep networks, improves upon DeepLIFT and shows better alignment with human intuition in user studies.
papers.limitation: Exact computation of SHAP values is challenging and requires approximations, which may rely on assumptions like feature independence and model linearity.
future_direction: Developing faster model-type-specific estimation methods that make fewer assumptions.
Integrating work on estimating interaction effects from game theory.
Defining new explanation model classes.
papers.abstract: Deep learning (DL) models find increasing application in mental state decoding, where researchers seek to understand the mapping between mental states (e.g., experiencing anger or joy) and brain activity by identifying those spatial and temporal features of brain activity that allow to accurately identify (i.e., decode) these states. Once a DL model has been trained to accurately decode a set of mental states, neuroimaging researchers often make use of methods from explainable artificial intelligence research to understand the model's learned mappings between mental states and brain activity. Here, we benchmark prominent explanation methods in a mental state decoding analysis of multiple functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) datasets. Our findings demonstrate a gradient between two key characteristics of an explanation in mental state decoding, namely, its faithfulness and its alignment with other empirical evidence on the mapping between brain activity and decoded mental state: explanation methods with high explanation faithfulness, which capture the model's decision process well, generally provide explanations that align less well with other empirical evidence than the explanations of methods with less faithfulness. Based on our findings, we provide guidance for neuroimaging researchers on how to choose an explanation method to gain insight into the mental state decoding decisions of DL models.

papers.title: Attention Heads of Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.core_contribution: This survey paper provides a comprehensive review of research on attention heads in large language models, introducing a novel four-stage framework (Knowledge Recalling, In-Context Identification, Latent Reasoning, Expression Preparation) to categorize attention head functions and summarizing experimental methods for discovering such heads.
papers.conclusion: The survey consolidates research on attention heads in LLMs, providing a framework for understanding their functions and the methods used to discover them, while highlighting the need for further work on complex tasks, unified frameworks, alignment with human cognition, generalizability, multi-collaboration, and theoretical support.
papers.key_findings:
The paper proposes a four-stage framework (Knowledge Recalling, In-Context Identification, Latent Reasoning, Expression Preparation) inspired by human thought to categorize the functions of attention heads in LLMs.
It provides a detailed taxonomy of special attention heads, categorizing them by their roles in the four stages and the LLM architectures where they were discovered.
The survey summarizes experimental methodologies for discovering attention heads into two main categories: Modeling-Free (Modification-Based and Replacement-Based) and Modeling-Required (Training-Required and Training-Free).
It describes how attention heads collaborate across different stages to solve complex tasks, using the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task as an example.
The paper outlines current limitations in the field, such as a focus on simple tasks and lack of unified frameworks, and proposes future research directions.
papers.limitation:
Current research primarily focuses on simple tasks, leaving complex reasoning tasks underexplored.
There is a lack of unified frameworks to comprehensively describe the mechanisms of attention heads.
Aligning LLM mechanisms with human cognitive processes remains a significant challenge.
future_direction: Extending research to more complex tasks and real-world applications.
Developing unified frameworks to comprehensively describe attention head mechanisms.
Enhancing alignment between LLM mechanisms and human cognitive processes.
papers.abstract: Since the advent of ChatGPT, Large Language Models (LLMs) have excelled in various tasks but remain as black-box systems. Understanding the reasoning bottlenecks of LLMs has become a critical challenge, as these limitations are deeply tied to their internal architecture. Among these, attention heads have emerged as a focal point for investigating the underlying mechanics of LLMs. In this survey, we aim to demystify the internal reasoning processes of LLMs by systematically exploring the roles and mechanisms of attention heads. We first introduce a novel four-stage framework inspired by the human thought process: Knowledge Recalling, In-Context Identification, Latent Reasoning, and Expression Preparation. Using this framework, we comprehensively review existing research to identify and categorize the functions of specific attention heads. Additionally, we analyze the experimental methodologies used to discover these special heads, dividing them into two categories: Modeling-Free and Modeling-Required methods. We further summarize relevant evaluation methods and benchmarks. Finally, we discuss the limitations of current research and propose several potential future directions.

papers.title: Factual Self-Awareness in Language Models: Representation, Robustness, and Scaling
papers.research_question: Do language models have an internal compass that dictates the correctness of factual recall at the time of generation? Specifically, are there linear features in the Transformer's residual stream that indicate whether the model will recall a correct attribute?
papers.core_contribution: Language models encode linear features in the residual stream that indicate whether they will correctly recall a factual attribute, and this self-awareness signal is robust to formatting variations and emerges early in training.
papers.conclusion: Language models possess intrinsic self-monitoring capabilities for factual recall, which contributes to their interpretability and reliability.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) show that factual self-awareness is encoded as linear directions in the residual stream, separable between known and forgotten factual associations.
The self-awareness signal is robust to superficial perturbations like quotation marks, but sensitive to structural changes like rephrasing as questions.
The signal emerges rapidly during training and peaks in intermediate layers.
Larger models (within a family) do not necessarily have more linearly decodable self-awareness representations.
The class balance of known and forgotten samples depends on the sampling parameters (k, l) used to define them.
papers.limitation:
Defining knowledge at the entity level is a limitation: when an LM fabricates factual associations, it may invent attributes for a known entity.
Some input templates introduced spurious correlations due to their phrasing, which had to be excluded.
papers.abstract: Factual incorrectness in generated content is one of the primary concerns in ubiquitous deployment of large language models (LLMs). Prior findings suggest LLMs can (sometimes) detect factual incorrectness in their generated content (i.e., fact-checking post-generation). In this work, we provide evidence supporting the presence of LLMs' internal compass that dictate the correctness of factual recall at the time of generation. We demonstrate that for a given subject entity and a relation, LLMs internally encode linear features in the Transformer's residual stream that dictate whether it will be able to recall the correct attribute (that forms a valid entity-relation-attribute triplet). This self-awareness signal is robust to minor formatting variations. We investigate the effects of context perturbation via different example selection strategies. Scaling experiments across model sizes and training dynamics highlight that self-awareness emerges rapidly during training and peaks in intermediate layers. These findings uncover intrinsic self-monitoring capabilities within LLMs, contributing to their interpretability and reliability.

papers.title: Sycophancy Hides Linearly in the Attention Heads
papers.research_question: How are correct-to-incorrect sycophancy signals represented in language models, and can they be steered using linear interventions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that correct-to-incorrect sycophancy is most linearly separable in a sparse subset of middle-layer attention heads, and that steering these heads with linear interventions effectively reduces sycophantic shifts.
papers.conclusion: The results indicate that attention-level activations are a practical and interpretable locus for mitigating sycophancy with simple, linear interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Sycophancy signals are detectable and steerable using simple linear probes.
These signals are most linearly separable and steerable in a sparse subset of middle-layer multi-head attention (MHA) heads, compared to the residual stream or MLP layers.
The influential sycophancy heads attend disproportionately to user disagreement tokens and sycophantic expressions in the dialogue.
The sycophancy direction is distinct from the previously identified 'truthful' direction, suggesting factual accuracy and deference resistance arise from related but distinct mechanisms.
Linear interventions on the identified attention heads can mitigate sycophantic behavior while preserving factual accuracy.
papers.limitation:
Evaluations are restricted to Gemma-3 and Llama-3.2 models.
Focus is primarily on correctness-preserving behavior and direct measures of sycophancy reduction; broader impacts on generation style and other alignment dimensions remain outside the current scope.
Attention patterns are used as diagnostic correlation rather than exhaustive accounts of the decision process.
future_direction: Investigating additional model sizes and architectures.
Studying broader impacts on generation style and other alignment dimensions.
Performing multi-objective steering.
papers.abstract: We find that correct-to-incorrect sycophancy signals are most linearly separable within multi-head attention activations. Motivated by the linear representation hypothesis, we train linear probes across the residual stream, multilayer perceptron (MLP), and attention layers to analyze where these signals emerge. Although separability appears in the residual stream and MLPs, steering using these probes is most effective in a sparse subset of middle-layer attention heads. Using TruthfulQA as the base dataset, we find that probes trained on it transfer effectively to other factual QA benchmarks. Furthermore, comparing our discovered direction to previously identified "truthful" directions reveals limited overlap, suggesting that factual accuracy, and deference resistance, arise from related but distinct mechanisms. Attention-pattern analysis further indicates that the influential heads attend disproportionately to expressions of user doubt, contributing to sycophantic shifts. Overall, these findings suggest that sycophancy can be mitigated through simple, targeted linear interventions that exploit the internal geometry of attention activations.

papers.title: Associative memory inspires improvements for in-context learning using a novel attention residual stream architecture
papers.research_question: How can insights from associative memory models be used to improve in-context learning (ICL) in Transformer-based language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel residual attention stream architecture, inspired by associative memory, that allows information to flow directly between attention heads, leading to faster and improved in-context learning in Transformers.
papers.conclusion: The residual attention stream architecture, inspired by associative memory models, improves in-context learning in Transformers and shows promising scalability to larger language models.
papers.key_findings:
A one-layer associative memory model (AMICL) can perform in-context learning on a classification task.
Adding a residual stream for attention values (and to a lesser extent, queries) in a two-layer Transformer speeds up the emergence of ICL during training compared to a classic Transformer.
Naively applying the residual value stream architecture to small language models (8M and 1B parameters) trained on Tiny Stories indicates performance improvements scale to larger models and more naturalistic data.
future_direction: Testing the residual attention stream architecture on larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the interpretability of the residual stream for understanding model mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate an impressive ability to utilise information within the context of their input sequences to appropriately respond to data unseen by the LLM during its training procedure. This ability is known as in-context learning (ICL). Humans and non-human animals demonstrate similar abilities, however their neural architectures differ substantially from LLMs. Despite this, a critical component within LLMs, the attention mechanism, resembles modern associative memory models, widely used in and influenced by the computational neuroscience community to model biological memory systems. Using this connection, we introduce an associative memory model capable of performing ICL. We use this as inspiration for a novel residual stream architecture which allows information to directly flow between attention heads. We test this architecture during training within a two-layer Transformer and show its ICL abilities manifest more quickly than without this modification. We then apply our architecture in small language models with 8 million and 1 billion parameters, focusing on attention head values, with results also indicating improved performance at these larger and more naturalistic scales.

papers.title: Linear Representations of Political Perspective Emerge in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the activation space of LLMs contain linear representations of political perspective, and can these be used to monitor and steer model outputs?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs possess linear representations of political ideology in their activation space, which can be identified through probing and used to monitor and steer model outputs.
papers.conclusion: LLMs learn linear representations of political perspective, enabling monitoring and steering of ideological slant in generated text.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes on attention heads can predict U.S. lawmakers' political ideology (DW-NOMINATE scores) with high Spearman correlation (up to ~0.87).
The representations are linear, as non-linear probes do not substantially improve predictive performance.
Probes trained on lawmakers' ideology generalize to predict the political slant of news outlets (Ad Fontes scores).
The learned linear directions can be used to monitor the political slant of generated text token-by-token.
Applying linear interventions to the identified attention heads can steer model outputs toward more liberal or conservative perspectives.
papers.limitation:
The generality of political slant representations varies significantly across nations, with weaker performance for non-U.S. contexts.
Extreme intervention values (alpha < -30 or > 30) often lead to incoherent model outputs.
future_direction: Creation of comprehensive datasets capturing diverse political contexts to improve cross-cultural applicability.
More systematic evaluation of the token-by-token monitoring method.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated the ability to generate text that realistically reflects a range of different subjective human perspectives. This paper studies how LLMs are seemingly able to reflect more liberal versus more conservative viewpoints among other political perspectives in American politics. We show that LLMs possess linear representations of political perspectives within activation space, wherein more similar perspectives are represented closer together. To do so, we probe the attention heads across the layers of three open transformer-based LLMs (Llama-2-7b-chat, Mistral-7b-instruct, Vicuna-7b). We first prompt models to generate text from the perspectives of different U.S. lawmakers. We then identify sets of attention heads whose activations linearly predict those lawmakers' DW-NOMINATE scores, a widely-used and validated measure of political ideology. We find that highly predictive heads are primarily located in the middle layers, often speculated to encode high-level concepts and tasks. Using probes only trained to predict lawmakers' ideology, we then show that the same probes can predict measures of news outlets' slant from the activations of models prompted to simulate text from those news outlets. These linear probes allow us to visualize, interpret, and monitor ideological stances implicitly adopted by an LLM as it generates open-ended responses. Finally, we demonstrate that by applying linear interventions to these attention heads, we can steer the model outputs toward a more liberal or conservative stance. Overall, our research suggests that LLMs possess a high-level linear representation of American political ideology and that by leveraging recent advances in mechanistic interpretability, we can identify, monitor, and steer the subjective perspective underlying generated text.

papers.title: LLM Assertiveness can be Mechanistically Decomposed into Emotional and Logical Components
papers.research_question: What is the internal basis of LLM assertiveness, and can it be decomposed into separable components like emotional and logical persuasion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLM assertiveness can be mechanistically decomposed into orthogonal emotional and logical components, providing evidence for a multi-component structure similar to human persuasion models.
papers.conclusion: The study provides mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlights avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers (5-6) are most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts.
High-assertive representations decompose into orthogonal emotional and logical clusters.
Emotional steering vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, whereas logical vectors have more localized effects.
papers.limitation:
The model is small (1B parameters), so scaling effects are uncertain.
Only one architecture is examined, limiting cross-model generality.
Dataset size is modest (n=645), which may obscure finer-grained cues.
Cluster interpretation relies on manual inspection.
future_direction: Develop more automated approaches for cluster interpretation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often display overconfidence, presenting information with unwarranted certainty in high-stakes contexts. We investigate the internal basis of this behavior via mechanistic interpretability. Using open-sourced Llama 3.2 models fine-tuned on human annotated assertiveness datasets, we extract residual activations across all layers, and compute similarity metrics to localize assertive representations. Our analysis identifies layers most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts and reveals that high-assertive representations decompose into two orthogonal sub-components of emotional and logical clusters-paralleling the dual-route Elaboration Likelihood Model in Psychology. Steering vectors derived from these sub-components show distinct causal effects: emotional vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, while logical vectors exert more localized effects. These findings provide mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlight avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.

papers.title: Plausibility Processing in Transformer Language Models: Focusing on the Role of Attention Heads in GPT
papers.research_question: How do Transformer language models process semantic knowledge, specifically the plausibility of noun-verb relations, and what is the causal role of attention heads in this processing?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that GPT2 processes noun-verb plausibility similarly to humans and identifies a set of attention heads that detect plausibility. It shows these heads collectively and causally contribute to the model's plausibility processing, with contributions being imbalanced and not strictly correlated with individual head performance.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that semantic plausibility knowledge in GPT2 is processed by a diffusely distributed set of attention heads that make imbalanced but collective causal contributions, highlighting the importance of causal analysis in understanding attention head functions.
papers.key_findings:
GPT2 exhibits a higher degree of similarity with humans in plausibility processing compared to other Transformer models (BERT, RoBERTa, ALBERT).
GPT2 contains 18 attention heads distributed across layers that are sensitive to noun-verb plausibility, independent of syntactic dependency.
Pruning these plausibility-processing heads eliminates GPT2's plausibility sensitivity, while pruning a random set of heads does not.
The causal contribution of individual plausibility-processing heads to the model's overall ability is imbalanced; a single head (0,10) accounts for a large portion of the effect for syntactic dependents.
The performance of an attention head in detecting plausibility (accuracy) does not necessarily correlate with its causal contribution to the model's overall plausibility processing ability.
papers.limitation:
The scope of the study is restricted to the plausibility of noun-verb relations, not covering other types of semantic knowledge.
The study does not detail how attention heads interact with other components like hidden states across layers or feed-forward networks.
future_direction: Expand the study's scope to a broader array of semantic knowledge for better generalizability.
Investigate interactions between attention heads and other model components (e.g., hidden states, feed-forward networks) to better understand their role in semantic knowledge processing.
papers.abstract: The goal of this paper is to explore how Transformer language models process semantic knowledge, especially regarding the plausibility of noun-verb relations. First, I demonstrate GPT2 exhibits a higher degree of similarity with humans in plausibility processing compared to other Transformer language models. Next, I delve into how knowledge of plausibility is contained within attention heads of GPT2 and how these heads causally contribute to GPT2's plausibility processing ability. Through several experiments, it was found that: i) GPT2 has a number of attention heads that detect plausible noun-verb relationships; ii) these heads collectively contribute to the Transformer's ability to process plausibility, albeit to varying degrees; and iii) attention heads' individual performance in detecting plausibility does not necessarily correlate with how much they contribute to GPT2's plausibility processing ability.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: The Other Mind: How Language Models Exhibit Human Temporal Cognition
papers.research_question: How do large language models exhibit human-like temporal cognition, specifically whether they spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point and adhere to the Weber-Fechner law?
papers.core_contribution: Larger LLMs spontaneously exhibit human-like temporal cognition, establishing a subjective reference point and adhering to the Weber-Fechner law, which emerges from multi-level convergence at neuronal, representational, and informational levels.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit human-like temporal cognition through multi-level convergence, suggesting cognition is a subjective construction of the external world. This points to the risk of alien cognitive frameworks and the need for AI alignment paradigms that guide internal world-building.
papers.key_findings:
In similarity judgment tasks, larger models spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point (ca. 2025) and their perception of time logarithmically compresses as years recede from this point, adhering to the Weber-Fechner law.
A subgroup of temporal-preferential neurons in the FFN exhibits minimal activation at the subjective reference point and implements a logarithmic coding scheme similar to biological systems.
Representations of years undergo hierarchical construction: from basic numerical values in shallow layers to abstract temporal orientation organized around a reference point in deep layers.
Pre-trained embedding models reveal that the training corpus possesses an inherent, non-linear temporal structure, providing raw material for the model's internal construction of temporal cognition.
The findings support an experientialist perspective where LLM cognition is a subjective construction of the external world by its internal representational system, leading to potential convergence with or divergence from human cognition.
future_direction: Evolve AI alignment beyond behavioral control to a paradigm that actively guides the formation of a model's internal world from its source.
Monitor models' emergent representational and cognitive patterns and enable intervention across the chain of cognition.
Curate the AI's environment with harmless or formalized verifiable information exposures.
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance, they exhibit certain cognitive patterns similar to those of humans that are not directly specified in training data. This study investigates this phenomenon by focusing on temporal cognition in LLMs. Leveraging the similarity judgment task, we find that larger models spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point and adhere to the Weber-Fechner law, whereby the perceived distance logarithmically compresses as years recede from this reference point. To uncover the mechanisms behind this behavior, we conducted multiple analyses across neuronal, representational, and informational levels. We first identify a set of temporal-preferential neurons and find that this group exhibits minimal activation at the subjective reference point and implements a logarithmic coding scheme convergently found in biological systems. Probing representations of years reveals a hierarchical construction process, where years evolve from basic numerical values in shallow layers to abstract temporal orientation in deep layers. Finally, using pre-trained embedding models, we found that the training corpus itself possesses an inherent, non-linear temporal structure, which provides the raw material for the model's internal construction. In discussion, we propose an experientialist perspective for understanding these findings, where the LLMs' cognition is viewed as a subjective construction of the external world by its internal representational system. This nuanced perspective implies the potential emergence of alien cognitive frameworks that humans cannot intuitively predict, pointing toward a direction for AI alignment that focuses on guiding internal constructions. Our code is available at https://TheOtherMind.github.io.

papers.title: Localizing Persona Representations in LLMs
papers.research_question: Where in the model are persona representations encoded, and how do these representations vary across different personas?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that persona representations in LLMs are most strongly encoded in the final third of decoder layers, with political ideologies having distinct activations while ethical perspectives show polysemantic overlap.
papers.conclusion: The study localizes persona representations in LLMs, showing encoding in later layers and differences in distinctiveness between political and ethical personas, which can inform model interpretability and control.
papers.key_findings:
Final third of layers capture the most variance in persona representations across multiple LLMs.
Political views have distinctly localized activations, while ethical values exhibit higher activation overlap.
Llama3 shows the largest separation across layers and personas.
Deep Scan identified salient activations that are useful for detecting persona-specific sentences.
Overlap in activations suggests polysemanticity in ethical representations.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is specific to selected datasets and may not generalize to other data sources.
Datasets are in English and reflect WEIRD perspectives, limiting cultural diversity.
future_direction: Explore a wider range of models and personas.
Incorporate beliefs from more diverse cultural contexts.
Investigate controlled modifications of internal representations.
papers.abstract: We present a study on how and where personas -- defined by distinct sets of human characteristics, values, and beliefs -- are encoded in the representation space of large language models (LLMs). Using a range of dimension reduction and pattern recognition methods, we first identify the model layers that show the greatest divergence in encoding these representations. We then analyze the activations within a selected layer to examine how specific personas are encoded relative to others, including their shared and distinct embedding spaces. We find that, across multiple pre-trained decoder-only LLMs, the analyzed personas show large differences in representation space only within the final third of the decoder layers. We observe overlapping activations for specific ethical perspectives -- such as moral nihilism and utilitarianism -- suggesting a degree of polysemy. In contrast, political ideologies like conservatism and liberalism appear to be represented in more distinct regions. These findings help to improve our understanding of how LLMs internally represent information and can inform future efforts in refining the modulation of specific human traits in LLM outputs. Warning: This paper includes potentially offensive sample statements.

papers.title: Transformers represent belief state geometry in their residual stream
papers.research_question: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Specifically, is the structure given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process, and are belief states linearly represented in the residual stream?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical framework and empirical evidence that transformers trained on next-token prediction linearly represent the geometry of belief states (from the mixed-state presentation of the data-generating process) in their residual stream, even for complex fractal geometries, and that this representation captures information beyond local next-token predictions.
papers.conclusion: Transformers construct predictive representations that encode the complex geometry of belief updating over hidden states, capturing an inference process over the underlying structure of the data-generating process, which provides a concrete link between training data structure and internal model representations.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on data from hidden Markov models (HMMs) linearly represent the belief state geometry of the mixed-state presentation in their residual stream, as verified by linear regression.
The belief state representation emerges during training and is not an artifact, as shown by controls including cross-validation and shuffling.
For processes where distinct belief states share the same next-token distribution (e.g., RRXOR), the belief state geometry is not well represented in the final layer alone but is distributed across multiple layers of the residual stream.
The representation captures information about the entire future distribution, not just the next token, as demonstrated by comparing pairwise distances between belief states versus next-token probabilities.
The belief state geometry is robust to the choice of using pre- or post-layer normalization activations.
papers.limitation:
Experimental validation focused on small-scale systems (HMMs with 3-5 states and vocabularies of 2-3 tokens), a significant simplification compared to modern language models.
For realistic systems, the dimensionality of the belief state simplex would exceed the residual stream dimension, suggesting representation must be compressed; the nature of this compression is not understood.
Explicitly computing ground-truth belief states becomes intractable as the size of the minimal generating structure and context window length grows, requiring new methodologies for validation in larger settings.
The work is limited to the stationary ergodic setting, though the framework is expected to extend to non-stationary and non-ergodic processes.
The paper establishes the representation of belief states but does not test whether transformers implement a circuit for performing Bayesian updates.
future_direction: Extending the framework to non-stationary and non-ergodic processes, such as in-context learning.
Understanding how belief state geometry is compressed when the simplex dimension exceeds the residual stream dimension.
Investigating the mapping between belief states and features, which is likely complex and architecture-dependent.
papers.abstract: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Here, we present evidence that this structure is given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process. Leveraging the theory of optimal prediction, we anticipate and then find that belief states are linearly represented in the residual stream of transformers, even in cases where the predicted belief state geometry has highly nontrivial fractal structure. We investigate cases where the belief state geometry is represented in the final residual stream or distributed across the residual streams of multiple layers, providing a framework to explain these observations. Furthermore we demonstrate that the inferred belief states contain information about the entire future, beyond the local next-token prediction that the transformers are explicitly trained on. Our work provides a general framework connecting the structure of training data to the geometric structure of activations inside transformers.

papers.title: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind hallucinations in language models, specifically regarding entity recognition and knowledge awareness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers entity recognition directions in the representation space that encode knowledge awareness and shows they causally affect knowledge refusal and hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models have internal representations of knowledge awareness that affect refusal and hallucinations, and that chat fine-tuning repurposes this existing mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover directions in the representation space that detect whether the model recognizes an entity as known or unknown.
These entity recognition directions generalize across diverse entity types (players, movies, cities, songs).
The directions causally affect knowledge refusal: steering can induce the model to refuse on known entities or hallucinate on unknown entities.
The directions disrupt the attention of downstream heads in the factual recall circuit, suppressing attribute extraction.
Early entity recognition directions regulate the model's expression of knowledge uncertainty, and uncertainty directions are predictive of incorrect answers.
papers.limitation: The methodology for labeling entities as known or unknown might introduce inaccuracies, as the model could guess attributes or fail to recall specific attributes while knowing about the entity.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models are a widespread problem, yet the mechanisms behind whether models will hallucinate are poorly understood, limiting our ability to solve this problem. Using sparse autoencoders as an interpretability tool, we discover that a key part of these mechanisms is entity recognition, where the model detects if an entity is one it can recall facts about. Sparse autoencoders uncover meaningful directions in the representation space, these detect whether the model recognizes an entity, e.g. detecting it doesn't know about an athlete or a movie. This suggests that models can have self-knowledge: internal representations about their own capabilities. These directions are causally relevant: capable of steering the model to refuse to answer questions about known entities, or to hallucinate attributes of unknown entities when it would otherwise refuse. We demonstrate that despite the sparse autoencoders being trained on the base model, these directions have a causal effect on the chat model's refusal behavior, suggesting that chat finetuning has repurposed this existing mechanism. Furthermore, we provide an initial exploration into the mechanistic role of these directions in the model, finding that they disrupt the attention of downstream heads that typically move entity attributes to the final token.

papers.title: Predictive Coding or Just Feature Discovery? An Alternative Account of Why Language Models Fit Brain Data
papers.research_question: How related are the representations learned by neural language models, translation models, and language tagging tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to embed language representations into a low-dimensional space based on transferability, and shows that this embedding captures the hierarchical organization of language processing in the human brain.
papers.conclusion: The low-dimensional structure of language representations reflects the structure of language representations in the human brain, and the method provides a template for investigating relationships between linguistic and cognitive representations.
papers.key_findings:
The representation embedding matrix reveals a low-dimensional structure where language models and translation models interpolate between word embeddings, syntactic/semantic tasks, and future word embeddings.
The first dimension of this structure corresponds to a hierarchy from low-level to high-level language processing.
This first dimension maps onto the brain's language processing hierarchy, with early auditory areas explained by lower-level features and higher-order areas by later model layers.
The representation embeddings can predict which representations best explain brain activity in different regions.
Most pairs of representations are discriminable based on their brain activity patterns, indicating the embeddings capture brain representation structure.
papers.limitation:
The chosen set of representations may not capture the full diversity of the space.
The use of GloVe as the universal input representation may not be truly universal.
The use of linear networks may underestimate relatedness between tasks.
future_direction: Using an even larger number of representations to better map the space.
Using other universal spaces, such as directly using fMRI data as input.
Exploring regularized nonlinear models for the encoder-decoder networks.
papers.abstract: Many recent studies have shown that representations drawn from neural network language models are extremely effective at predicting brain responses to natural language. But why do these models work so well? One proposed explanation is that language models and brains are similar because they have the same objective: to predict upcoming words before they are perceived. This explanation is attractive because it lends support to the popular theory of predictive coding. We provide several analyses that cast doubt on this claim. First, we show that the ability to predict future words does not uniquely (or even best) explain why some representations are a better match to the brain than others. Second, we show that within a language model, representations that are best at predicting future words are strictly worse brain models than other representations. Finally, we argue in favor of an alternative explanation for the success of language models in neuroscience: These models are effective at predicting brain responses because they generally capture a wide variety of linguistic phenomena.

papers.title: Bias A-head? Analyzing Bias in Transformer-Based Language Model Attention Heads
papers.research_question: How does bias manifest and behave internally in a language model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a framework to identify biased attention heads in transformer-based language models and shows that biases are encoded in a small set of heads, which can be targeted for debiasing.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that biases in language models are encoded in a small set of attention heads, and the proposed framework helps understand and mitigate these biases, contributing to more transparent and fair NLP systems.
papers.key_findings:
Biased attention heads can be identified via gradient-based bias scores, and counter-stereotype experiments validate that these heads encode stereotypes.
The distribution of biased heads differs across models, with GPT-2 having fewer biased heads than BERT.
Masking out a small set of biased heads can reduce model bias with minimal impact on language modeling and NLU performance.
LLaMA-2-Chat exhibits less bias than LLaMA-2, suggesting that RLHF reduces stereotyping.
Prior debiasing strategies may cover up bias rather than remove it, as some anti-bias heads are turned into biased heads after debiasing.
papers.limitation:
Focuses only on stereotyping bias (representational harm) and not allocational bias.
Relies on existing word lists which may have limited coverage for other protected groups and non-English languages.
Focuses on attention heads only, while bias may also manifest in other model components.
Does not investigate heads with negative bias scores (anti-bias heads) in detail.
future_direction: Apply the method to assess biases in larger foundation models like GPT-3 and LLaMA.
Study allocational bias in downstream NLP tasks.
Investigate other model components and anti-bias heads for a more comprehensive understanding.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based pretrained large language models (PLM) such as BERT and GPT have achieved remarkable success in NLP tasks. However, PLMs are prone to encoding stereotypical biases. Although a burgeoning literature has emerged on stereotypical bias mitigation in PLMs, such as work on debiasing gender and racial stereotyping, how such biases manifest and behave internally within PLMs remains largely unknown. Understanding the internal stereotyping mechanisms may allow better assessment of model fairness and guide the development of effective mitigation strategies. In this work, we focus on attention heads, a major component of the Transformer architecture, and propose a bias analysis framework to explore and identify a small set of biased heads that are found to contribute to a PLM's stereotypical bias. We conduct extensive experiments to validate the existence of these biased heads and to better understand how they behave. We investigate gender and racial bias in the English language in two types of Transformer-based PLMs: the encoder-based BERT model and the decoder-based autoregressive GPT model. Overall, the results shed light on understanding the bias behavior in pretrained language models.

papers.title: Latent Introspection: Models Can Detect Prior Concept Injections
papers.research_question: Can language models access information about their own prior internal states? Specifically, can they detect when concepts have been injected into their earlier context and identify which concept was injected?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that open-weight language models possess a latent capacity for introspection, enabling them to detect prior concept injections. This ability is often hidden in the residual stream and can be dramatically strengthened through specific prompting.
papers.conclusion: Language models have a surprising capacity for introspection and steering awareness that is easy to overlook, with consequences for latent reasoning and safety.
papers.key_findings:
Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct can detect prior concept injections, with detection signals emerging in middle layers (50–60) but attenuating in the final layers before output.
Prompting the model with accurate information about AI introspection mechanisms can increase detection sensitivity from 0.3% to 39.9% with only a 0.6% increase in false positives.
The model can identify which of nine concepts was injected earlier, with mutual information between injected and recovered concepts rising from 0.61 bits to 1.05 bits, ruling out generic noise explanations.
Detection capacity varies dramatically with prompting; a vague framing outperforms a mechanistically accurate description, achieving up to 84.0% accuracy.
The phenomenon generalizes to larger models (Llama 3.3 70B Instruct and Qwen 2.5 72B Instruct), though with different prompt sensitivities and signal strengths.
papers.limitation: The introspection signals are suppressed in the final layers of the model, which may be due to post-training effects (e.g., safety training), pretraining factors, or distribution shift.
future_direction: Distinguishing the causes of late-layer suppression (post-training vs. pretraining effects).
Mechanistic investigation of why vague framing outperforms accurate description in prompting.
papers.abstract: We uncover a latent capacity for introspection in a Qwen 32B model, demonstrating that the model can detect when concepts have been injected into its earlier context and identify which concept was injected. While the model denies injection in sampled outputs, logit lens analysis reveals clear detection signals in the residual stream, which are attenuated in the final layers. Furthermore, prompting the model with accurate information about AI introspection mechanisms can dramatically strengthen this effect: the sensitivity to injection increases massively (0.3% -> 39.2%) with only a 0.6% increase in false positives. Also, mutual information between nine injected and recovered concepts rises from 0.62 bits to 1.05 bits, ruling out generic noise explanations. Our results demonstrate models can have a surprising capacity for introspection and steering awareness that is easy to overlook, with consequences for latent reasoning and safety.

papers.title: Brain-Language Model Alignment: Insights into the Platonic Hypothesis and Intermediate-Layer Advantage
papers.research_question: Do brains and language models converge toward the same internal representations of the world? The paper reviews evidence to test the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and the Intermediate-Layer Advantage.
papers.core_contribution: This review of 25 fMRI-based studies provides converging evidence that models and brains may share abstract representational structures, supporting the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and the Intermediate-Layer Advantage.
papers.conclusion: Framing alignment through the dual lenses of the PRH and the Intermediate-Layer Advantage provides a theoretical scaffold for designing future experiments, benchmarks, and models that more directly probe shared human–artificial representational structure.
papers.key_findings:
Alignment tends to be stronger for larger, higher-performing models and those trained on more tasks, supporting the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.
Cross-modal training reliably enhances alignment by pushing models toward modality-independent conceptual representations.
Intermediate layers of language models show the strongest alignment with brain activity, supporting the Intermediate-Layer Advantage.
Fine-tuning (including instruction-tuning and brain-tuning) can improve alignment, but the evidence is not uniformly positive.
Multimodal models, especially vision-language models, align better with brain activity than unimodal models.
papers.limitation: The studies analysed differ in metrics, datasets, and alignment protocols. Such heterogeneity implies that effects of scale or layer depth should be treated as qualitative patterns rather than quantitative laws.
future_direction: Designing future experiments, benchmarks, and models that more directly probe shared human–artificial representational structure.
papers.abstract: Do brains and language models converge toward the same internal representations of the world? Recent years have seen a rise in studies of neural activations and model alignment. In this work, we review 25 fMRI-based studies published between 2023 and 2025 and explicitly confront their findings with two key hypotheses: (i) the Platonic Representation Hypothesis -- that as models scale and improve, they converge to a representation of the real world, and (ii) the Intermediate-Layer Advantage -- that intermediate (mid-depth) layers often encode richer, more generalizable features. Our findings provide converging evidence that models and brains may share abstract representational structures, supporting both hypotheses and motivating further research on brain-model alignment.

papers.title: Visualizing Attention in Transformer-Based Language Representation Models
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents an open-source visualization tool for multi-head self-attention in Transformer-based language models, extending prior work with three granularity levels (attention-head, model, and neuron views) and demonstrating its use on BERT and GPT-2.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a tool for visualizing attention in Transformer-based language models, demonstrates its application on BERT and GPT-2, and outlines future work including empirical evaluation and interface integration.
papers.key_findings:
The tool can visualize attention patterns at three levels, revealing positional and lexical patterns in attention heads.
The attention-head view can be used to detect potential model bias, such as gender bias in coreference resolution in GPT-2.
The model view can identify recurring patterns, such as null attention to the first token, suggesting a potential design improvement.
The neuron view can link specific neurons in the query and key vectors to model behavior, such as a distance-decaying attention pattern.
The tool provides actionable insights for model interpretation and potential intervention, such as manipulating neurons to control attention behavior.
future_direction: Empirically evaluate how attention impacts model predictions across a range of tasks.
Integrate the three views (attention-head, model, neuron) into a unified interface.
Visualize the value vectors in addition to the queries and keys, and enable users to manipulate the model by modifying attention or editing individual neurons.
papers.abstract: We present an open-source tool for visualizing multi-head self-attention in Transformer-based language representation models. The tool extends earlier work by visualizing attention at three levels of granularity: the attention-head level, the model level, and the neuron level. We describe how each of these views can help to interpret the model, and we demonstrate the tool on the BERT model and the OpenAI GPT-2 model. We also present three use cases for analyzing GPT-2: detecting model bias, identifying recurring patterns, and linking neurons to model behavior.

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how post-training affects LLMs internally, revealing which mechanisms are preserved (e.g., knowledge storage locations, truthfulness direction) and which are altered (e.g., refusal direction), with implications for model steering and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Post-training preserves some internal mechanisms (like knowledge storage and truthfulness direction) and alters others (like refusal direction), providing insights for model steering and future research in interpretability and LLM post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations in LLMs.
Post-training adapts knowledge representations from the base model while also developing new ones.
The truthfulness direction is highly similar between base and post-trained models and is effectively transferable for interventions.
The refusal direction differs between base and post-trained models and shows limited forward transferability.
Differences in confidence between base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons.
papers.limitation: Complex, multi-step processes such as reasoning and instruction-following are not well-captured by current mechanistic interpretability tools, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Design better post-training methods based on mechanistic insights.
Extend analysis to other capabilities like reasoning and instruction-following.
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for the success of large language models (LLMs), transforming pre-trained base models into more useful and aligned post-trained models. While plenty of works have studied post-training algorithms and evaluated post-training models by their outputs, it remains understudied how post-training reshapes LLMs internally. In this paper, we compare base and post-trained LLMs mechanistically from four perspectives to better understand post-training effects. Our findings across model families and datasets reveal that: (1) Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations, and it adapts knowledge representations from the base model while developing new knowledge representations; (2) Both truthfulness and refusal can be represented by vectors in the hidden representation space. The truthfulness direction is highly similar between the base and post-trained model, and it is effectively transferable for interventions; (3) The refusal direction is different between the base and post-trained models, and it shows limited forward transferability; (4) Differences in confidence between the base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons. Our study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms preserved and altered during post-training, facilitates downstream tasks like model steering, and could potentially benefit future research in interpretability and LLM post-training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HZD01/post-training-mechanistic-analysis.

papers.title: Correspondence between the layered structure of deep language models and temporal structure of natural language processing in the human brain
papers.research_question: Does the layered hierarchy of deep language models (DLMs) correspond to the temporal dynamics of language comprehension in the human brain? Specifically, is there a correlation between DLM layer depth and the time at which layers are most predictive of human brain activity?
papers.core_contribution: The layered hierarchy of deep language models (specifically GPT2-XL) corresponds to the temporal dynamics of language comprehension in the human brain, with early layers predicting early neural responses and later layers predicting later responses in high-order language areas.
papers.conclusion: The internal sequence of computations across layers in deep language models models the temporal hierarchy of language comprehension in the human brain, providing evidence for shared computational principles between DLMs and the brain.
papers.key_findings:
There is a strong positive correlation (Pearson r=0.85 in IFG) between DLM layer depth and the time of peak encoding performance in high-order language areas (IFG, TP, aSTG).
Intermediate layers of GPT2-XL (e.g., layer 22 in IFG) provide the best overall prediction of neural activity across language areas, forming an inverted U-shaped curve.
For predictable words, the temporal sequence is clear; for unpredictable words, the pattern is weaker and early layers shift to later lags (around 300ms) in IFG.
The temporal progression timescale increases along the ventral linguistic hierarchy, with the largest within-ROI temporal separation in the Temporal Pole (over 500 ms).
The observed lag-layer correlation is due to nonlinear transformations in the DLM, as linear interpolations between first and last layer embeddings yield significantly lower correlations.
papers.limitation:
The study uses a single DLM (GPT2-XL) and a single narrative stimulus, limiting generalizability.
The temporal resolution of the ECoG measurements, although high, was binned at 50 ms, which may not disambiguate layers that peak at similar times.
The hierarchical structure of DLMs is spatial, while that of the brain is spatiotemporal, representing a fundamental architectural difference.
future_direction: Explore other model architectures (e.g., recurrent, convolutional, or models with explicit temporal dynamics) to see if they better capture brain dynamics.
Use longer contexts and more diverse stimuli to test the robustness of the layer-time correspondence.
Investigate how DLMs might be augmented (e.g., with recurrence or explicit temporal hierarchies) to better model the brain's spatiotemporal language processing.
papers.abstract: Abstract Deep language models (DLMs) provide a novel computational paradigm for how the brain processes natural language. Unlike symbolic, rule-based models described in psycholinguistics, DLMs encode words and their context as continuous numerical vectors. These “embeddings” are constructed by a sequence of computations organized in “layers” to ultimately capture surprisingly sophisticated representations of linguistic structures. How does this layered hierarchy map onto the human brain during natural language comprehension? In this study, we used electrocorticography (ECoG) to record neural activity in language areas along the superior temporal gyrus and inferior frontal gyrus while human participants listened to a 30-minute spoken narrative. We supplied this same narrative to a high-performing DLM (GPT2-XL) and extracted the contextual embeddings for each word in the story across all 48 layers of the model. We next trained a set of linear encoding models to predict the temporally-evolving neural activity from the embeddings at each layer. We found a striking correspondence between the layer-by-layer sequence of embeddings from GPT2-XL and the temporal sequence of neural activity in language areas. In addition, we found evidence for the gradual accumulation of recurrent information along the linguistic processing hierarchy. However, we also noticed additional neural processes in the brain, but not in DLMs, during the processing of surprising (unpredictable) words. These findings point to a connection between human language processing and DLMs where the layer-by-layer accumulation of contextual information in DLM embeddings matches the temporal dynamics of neural activity in high-order language areas.

papers.title: Tracing Facts or just Copies? A critical investigation of the Competitions of Mechanisms in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in LLMs mediate the competition between factual recall from parametric memory and counterfactual information provided in context? Do they perform selective counterfactual suppression or general copy suppression, and are they domain-specific?
papers.core_contribution: Attention heads that promote factual output in LLMs operate via general copy suppression rather than selective counterfactual suppression, and their behavior is domain-dependent, with larger models showing more specialization.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms that attention heads mediate the competition between factual and counterfactual tokens via copy suppression, and their effects are domain-dependent, with implications for model interpretability and control.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads contribute to the competition between factual and counterfactual tokens, and modifying their strength affects the proportion of factual outputs.
The attention heads supporting factual tokens suppress copying in general, not just counterfactuals, as they also suppress factual tokens when facts are present in the prompt.
The effect of attention heads is sensitive to sentence structure and the presence of hints (factual token in the subject).
Attention heads exhibit domain specialization; their contribution varies by answer category (e.g., location, language, organization).
Larger models (Pythia-6.9B) show more specialized and category-sensitive patterns than smaller models (GPT-2).
papers.limitation: The experiments are limited to two models (GPT-2 and Pythia-6.9B) and do not cover more models or study attention modification of different heads on different domains in detail.
future_direction: Applying the methods to different models
Studying how each attention head interacts with different domains
Constructing new datasets on other domains (e.g., STEM) and applying similar techniques
papers.abstract: This paper presents a reproducibility study examining how Large Language Models (LLMs) manage competing factual and counterfactual information, focusing on the role of attention heads in this process. We attempt to reproduce and reconcile findings from three recent studies by Ortu et al., Yu, Merullo, and Pavlick and McDougall et al. that investigate the competition between model-learned facts and contradictory context information through Mechanistic Interpretability tools. Our study specifically examines the relationship between attention head strength and factual output ratios, evaluates competing hypotheses about attention heads' suppression mechanisms, and investigates the domain specificity of these attention patterns. Our findings suggest that attention heads promoting factual output do so via general copy suppression rather than selective counterfactual suppression, as strengthening them can also inhibit correct facts. Additionally, we show that attention head behavior is domain-dependent, with larger models exhibiting more specialized and category-sensitive patterns.

papers.title: Interpretability for Multimodal Emotion Recognition using Concept Activation Vectors
papers.research_question: How can the reasoning process of neural networks for emotion recognition be represented using human-understandable concepts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends the Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV) method to multimodal (video, audio, text) emotion recognition and proposes novel human-understandable concepts for interpreting emotion recognition models, showing that neural networks use these concepts for classification.
papers.conclusion: DNNs for emotion recognition make use of human-understandable concepts for classification, and interpretability for emotion recognition can be achieved using Concept Activation Vectors.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed concepts (Variations in Physiognomy, Voice Pitch, Utterance Polarity) are significant for interpretability of emotion recognition.
The influence of concepts varies across emotion classes and across unimodal and multimodal levels of the network.
There is no single concept that is significant for all emotions, which aligns with the human perspective on emotion recognition.
The BC-LSTM network's reasoning process for emotion recognition can be represented using human-understandable concepts.
papers.limitation:
The BC-LSTM network is relatively simple compared to state-of-the-art models, and the concept sets are approximations based on general assumptions.
Dataset bias (models perform better on text input) could affect interpretation.
future_direction: Extending the TCAV method to more complex architectures.
Discovering emotion-related concepts in an unsupervised setting to reduce human annotation effort.
papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition refers to the classification of input video sequences into emotion labels based on multiple input modalities (usually video, audio and text). In recent years, Deep Neural networks have shown remarkable performance in recognizing human emotions, and are on par with human-level performance on this task. Despite the recent advancements in this field, emotion recognition systems are yet to be accepted for real world setups due to the obscure nature of their reasoning and decision-making process. Most of the research in this field deals with novel architectures to improve the performance for this task, with a few attempts at providing explanations for these models' decisions. In this paper, we address the issue of interpretability for neural networks in the context of emotion recognition using Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs). To analyse the model's latent space, we define human-understandable concepts specific to Emotion AI and map them to the widely-used IEMOCAP multimodal database. We then evaluate the influence of our proposed concepts at multiple layers of the Bi-directional Contextual LSTM (BC-LSTM) network to show that the reasoning process of neural networks for emotion recognition can be represented using human-understandable concepts. Finally, we perform hypothesis testing on our proposed concepts to show that they are significant for interpretability of this task.

papers.title: Transferring Linear Features Across Language Models With Model Stitching
papers.research_question: Can linear features (e.g., from Sparse Autoencoders, probes, and steering vectors) be transferred between language models of different sizes using affine mappings (model stitching), and what are the implications for efficiency and feature universality?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that affine mappings (stitches) between residual streams can effectively transfer linear features across language models, enabling compute-efficient training of Sparse Autoencoders and transfer of probes and steering vectors, while revealing differences in how semantic and structural features transfer.
papers.conclusion: Linear features can be transferred between language models via affine mappings, supporting weak universality and providing a method to improve the training efficiency of interpretability tools like Sparse Autoencoders.
papers.key_findings:
Using transferred SAEs as initialization can reduce FLOPs by ~50% when training SAEs on larger models.
Probes and steering vectors can be transferred between models with no additional training in specific cases (e.g., language steering).
Structural features (syntactic) transfer more consistently than semantic features, which are more polarized in transferability.
Specific functional features (e.g., entropy and attention deactivation features) preserve their roles after transfer.
Linear stitches support a weak universality hypothesis, showing that small and large models learn similar representation spaces.
papers.limitation:
Stitches are only trained on general internet text between models in the same family with the same tokenizer.
The scaling law analysis is theoretically incomplete due to lack of high-compute regime data to fit the irreducible loss.
The semantic/structural classification is imperfect and noisy due to reliance on another LLM for augmentations.
Probing and steering experiments are limited to particular tasks and settings.
future_direction: Verify findings in cross-family model settings and finetune stitches on special tokens or chat-templated data.
Explore other applications of stitches, such as transferring linear weight updates like LoRAs.
Expand probing and steering experiments to examine robustness and broader task settings.
papers.abstract: In this work, we demonstrate that affine mappings between residual streams of language models is a cheap way to effectively transfer represented features between models. We apply this technique to transfer the weights of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) between models of different sizes to compare their representations. We find that small and large models learn similar representation spaces, which motivates training expensive components like SAEs on a smaller model and transferring to a larger model at a FLOPs savings. In particular, using a small-to-large transferred SAE as initialization can lead to 50% cheaper training runs when training SAEs on larger models. Next, we show that transferred probes and steering vectors can effectively recover ground truth performance. Finally, we dive deeper into feature-level transferability, finding that semantic and structural features transfer noticeably differently while specific classes of functional features have their roles faithfully mapped. Overall, our findings illustrate similarities and differences in the linear representation spaces of small and large models and demonstrate a method for improving the training efficiency of SAEs.

papers.title: Does injecting linguistic structure into language models lead to better alignment with brain recordings?
papers.research_question: Does injecting linguistic structure into language models lead to better alignment with brain recordings?
papers.core_contribution: Injecting linguistic structure bias into language models via guided attention during fine-tuning can improve alignment with brain recordings, particularly for word-level fMRI data.
papers.conclusion: Injecting linguistic structure bias through guided attention can improve brain decoding performance, with clearer benefits for finer-grained (word-level) analyses, and highlights the importance of controlling for domain effects.
papers.key_findings:
For the word-level Wehbe2014 fMRI dataset, guided attention models significantly outperform pretrained and domain-finetuned baselines in brain decoding.
For the sentence-level Pereira2018 dataset, improvements are more modest, with UD and DM guided attention models showing some improvement over the pretrained baseline.
Domain of the fine-tuning data is an important confound affecting brain alignment; simply fine-tuning on a different domain can reduce alignment.
Guided attention models perform better on subject-verb agreement syntactic probing tasks, with performance ranking corresponding to brain decoding scores.
Guided attention improves performance on a semantic tagging task for most semantic categories, especially discourse and temporal relations.
papers.limitation:
The fMRI data was recorded during passive reading without a specific task, which may limit the ability to uncover fine-grained patterns of linguistic structure.
Potential confounds such as domain, corpus size, and dependency length differences between the linguistic formalisms are not fully controlled for due to the lack of a common annotated corpus.
future_direction: Investigating brain alignment using continuous, naturalistic listening fMRI datasets.
Using a common annotated corpus for all formalisms to properly control for confounds like domain and corpus size.
papers.abstract: Neuroscientists evaluate deep neural networks for natural language processing as possible candidate models for how language is processed in the brain. These models are often trained without explicit linguistic supervision, but have been shown to learn some linguistic structure in the absence of such supervision (Manning et al., 2020), potentially questioning the relevance of symbolic linguistic theories in modeling such cognitive processes (Warstadt and Bowman, 2020). We evaluate across two fMRI datasets whether language models align better with brain recordings, if their attention is biased by annotations from syntactic or semantic formalisms. Using structure from dependency or minimal recursion semantic annotations, we find alignments improve significantly for one of the datasets. For another dataset, we see more mixed results. We present an extensive analysis of these results.
